title: Jen Berrent — Covenant (founder) on structure, conflicts and legal data in private markets
author: Jen Berrent

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Berrent does not directly assess in-house AI adoption or selective insourcing. Instead, she shifts the focus to a provider-side strategy in which a law firm builds client-facing tools and productizes legal services to capture a larger share of client spending, while acknowledging conflicts as a structural constraint.
qs: it's not just a matter of hiring more lawyers, but it's actually building more tools for our clients to use.
And  we think law could have a similar feel if you productize, but we have a conflicts issue.

st.t: Expert workflows: Legal context becomes product infrastructure
st.an: Berrent accepts technology-enabled legal delivery and materially extends the cluster’s workflow proposition toward client-facing infrastructure: legal services should give clients continuing control over data through software interfaces, with AI and lawyers deliberately combined. She also adds that personal trust remains important even where later delivery involves substantially less human contact.
qs: But the delivery of legal services could provide control over data and information to those clients in an interface that's technology that looks like any other SAS product that HR or finance would have.
And so and then from there we sort of designed the business to have very specific solutions saying okay AI exists, lawyers exist and how are we going to marry those two?

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Berrent accepts the value of specialist legal workflow layers combining AI with lawyers, and materially extends the cluster by framing those systems around client-controlled interfaces, data access and service delivery rather than primarily lawyer-facing workflows. Her account remains founder observation rather than independent performance evidence.
qs: But the delivery of legal services could provide control over data and information to those clients in an interface that's technology that looks like any other SAS product that HR or finance would have.
And so and then from there we sort of designed the business to have very specific solutions saying okay AI exists, lawyers exist and how are we going to marry those two?

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Berrent accepts the organisational-redesign proposition and develops it through Covenant’s concrete model: client-facing technology that gives clients control over legal data, with delivery deliberately combining AI and lawyers. Her emphasis on relationship-based trust and incentives for a small founding team also identifies practical constraints on scaling this model, though she provides business reasoning rather than measured performance evidence.
qs: But the delivery of legal services could provide control over data and information to those clients in an interface that's technology that looks like any other SAS product that HR or finance would have.
And so and then from there we sort of designed the business to have very specific solutions saying okay AI exists, lawyers exist and how are we going to marry those two?

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Berrent accepts the cluster’s core proposition and supplies a concrete operating model for it: Covenant productises bounded investor-side workflows, uses AI rather than additional associates as leverage, retains lawyer verification, and charges per transaction. Her account materially develops the synthesis by showing how an AI-native legal-services provider can reorganise production and pricing while preserving lawyers for verification, advice and trust—although its efficiency and price claims remain company-reported.
qs: You don't actually need, you know, law firm associates reading that document that you need law firm associates for a lot of other things, but you don't need it for this process.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Berrent accepts the cluster’s human-led, task-selective model and materially extends it with a concrete operating design: multiple models review a bounded document-analysis task, disagreement directs lawyer verification, and the verified output becomes structured client-owned data. She also illustrates how this redesign can shift routine work from law firms to a technology-leveraged legal-service provider while preserving higher-value advisory roles.
qs: You don't actually need, you know, law firm associates reading that document that you need law firm associates for a lot of other things, but you don't need it for this process.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Berrent supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI-enabled legal change should be organised around clients rather than inherited law-firm workflows. Her division-of-labour framing is consistent with reallocating work, but the excerpt provides little detail on delivery design, pricing, verification, staffing or implementation, and its global emphasis is not developed enough to constitute a material extension.
qs: And I do think that for law to change, there needs to be a focus on the client experience, not on the law firm lawyer experience.

st.t: Legal data: Connected records enable operational transformation
st.an: Berrent directly supports the proposition that transforming legal documents into structured, usable data enables analysis and shifts knowledge access toward clients while retaining lawyer verification. Her evidence is an early-stage product and client-adoption account rather than quantified proof of operational outcomes.
qs: And all of a sudden now I have this complicated you know you know 100page plus document that is a lot of words that has now come into uh you know the format of data that I can graph I can compare I can you know think about I can see trends I can see outliers and that has just been you know sort of magnificent for clients to to start to experience that.

And we are seeing the appetite for our clients to have access to their own legal data is pretty amazing and that you know we're just in the infancy of that being sort of cost effective and  possible and that is taking sort of this idea of the gatekeeper and the owner of legal data and what's market being from outside council to being to a client and that is a very big shift.

kp.k: Designing legal services around AI rather than adding tools
kp.d: Berrent describes Covenant as an AI-powered law firm focused on private markets, designed from inception around AI and lawyers together. Her Amazon analogy concerns redesigning operating logistics around a new technology rather than adding technology to an existing business. The intended client experience extends beyond documents and emails to control over legal information through a software interface.
qs: we started a law firm with the premise that AI exists.
the delivery of legal services doesn't need to end with a you know a word document or an email.

kp.k: Narrow products target dramatic time and cost reductions
kp.d: Berrent says Covenant selects specific problems it can solve end to end, claiming decreases in time and cost of 80–90%, rather than marginal efficiencies from general-purpose tools. Its initial limited partnership agreement review offering expanded into investor-side investment document review, summarisation and issue spotting, alongside MFN election compendiums. These are founder-reported performance claims, not independently measured findings presented in the interview.
qs: that process just you know takes something and decreases the time cost by 80 90%.
we started with a wedge of doing limited partnership agreement review.
We really wanted to just take one problem and solve it dramatically for clients and that's what we've done with the MFN.

kp.k: Personal relationships remain essential to client acquisition
kp.d: Despite productised delivery, Berrent reports that clients arrive primarily through relationships rather than a product-led process. She or her co-founder still meets every client to establish confidence in quality and trustworthiness, although subsequent human contact may decline significantly.
qs: the clients come to us much less through um a productled process. It is much more relationship based still.
even if after that initial meeting the human contact actually may drop off significantly.

kp.k: Six lawyers use technology instead of staffing leverage
kp.d: Berrent reports a six-lawyer team with high work capacity and explicitly describes AI, technology and focus as its leverage rather than additional people. This is her alternative to traditional staffing leverage, not a reported associate-to-partner ratio. Substantial product development underpins the model.
qs: So we're six lawyers, but it's highly highly leveraged, right?
the leverage is the AI the leverage is the technology the leverage is focus the leverage isn't the people

kp.k: Multiple-model review supports targeted human verification
kp.d: Berrent describes sending investment documents to multiple models using ensembling, exploiting the low marginal cost of another AI review. Lawyers verify the returned answers: agreement is said to make checking faster, while disagreement triggers deeper investigation. The source describes a human-verification workflow, without reporting measured accuracy or error rates.
qs: the marginal cost of an additional AI review is very low
So then we get those multiple model answers back and then the job of the lawyer to verify becomes easier
when the models disagree then you allow for sort of an additional layer of of uh sort of diving deep into it

kp.k: Longer context windows enabled the January 2024 launch
kp.d: Berrent attributes the viability of the initial LPA review product to larger context windows becoming available in November 2023, followed by an MVP built over the holiday period and launch in January 2024. She says earlier retrieval and chunking approaches lost too much quality on 120-page legal agreements, whose definitions, cross-references and nuance made human review faster.
qs: until November of 2023 the context window was not large enough
any other solution you know rag you know chunking just there's too much of a decrease in quality that the human was beating the machine
we launched in January 2024

kp.k: Capital funds client tools rather than more lawyers
kp.d: Berrent reports that client demand changed the development strategy from delivering reviews toward giving clients direct control over their legal information and tools. She says Covenant took external capital in the interview's relative timeframe of “this year” to fund product development, rather than simply expanding lawyer headcount.
qs: They see law firm lawyers using AI tools and they want to use AI tools.
They don't like law firms being the gatekeeper of their data.
we really needed capital for product development, right? it's not just a matter of hiring more lawyers, but it's actually building more tools for our clients to use.

kp.k: Sister companies separate legal practice and intellectual property
kp.d: In response to questions about investment and New York regulation, Berrent describes a New York law firm and a sister IP company holding the brand and technology, with a licence between them. She says the law firm's operating costs remain in the law firm. This is an account of Covenant's structure, not a legal determination about its regulatory compliance.
qs: we have sister companies. is it's a New York law firm.
there's an IP company and what's in that IP company is obviously brand but the all the technology but all of the costs of operating the law firm are in the law firm
there's a license between the two to use this technology.

kp.k: Conflicts constrain ambitions for comprehensive client adoption
kp.d: Berrent uses Salesforce as an analogy for capturing a client's entire share of a productised workflow, but identifies conflicts as a limit. Covenant represents only investors; using the technology for the other side would require a different law firm. She also describes interest in partnering with GP-side or company-side firms and says choosing one side supports client trust.
qs: we really believe that law could look like SAS in terms of share of wallet.
we have decided we will only do one side of that transaction in this law firm.
if we want to use the technology to represent the other side, that would have to be a different law firm

kp.k: Transaction-based fixed fees replace most hourly billing
kp.d: Berrent reports a $900 basic document review fee and fixed-fee supplements for greater lawyer involvement in live transactions, particularly where clients lack an in-house general counsel. She affirms the host's framing of approximately 90% lower prices for narrow work streams, while qualifying that some firms may charge less than her roughly tenfold comparison. No systematic fee comparison is supplied.
qs: We charge for our basic review charge $900.
maybe some law firms do it slightly less.
But again, that's based on a fixed fee. Almost nothing we do is by the hour.

kp.k: Specialist advice remains with complementary outside firms
kp.d: Berrent describes a deliberate decision not to add a tax lawyer, with tax and regulatory advice instead provided alongside clients' existing specialists. Keeping those services outside Covenant preserves its narrow, affordable offering. She argues that some document-processing work reaches traditional firms because clients lack another scalable, quality-assured destination, while acknowledging the continuing value of other associate work and bespoke advice.
qs: There's a lot of place to get really good bespoke tax advice. Our clients already have relationships with tax and regulatory.
you can work side by side with another law firm
you need law firm associates for a lot of other things, but you don't need it for this process.
You have lawyer verification.

kp.k: Recruitment combines AI conviction with financial rewards
kp.d: Berrent says the small team initially needs lawyers who believe AI is transformative and want to build something new, alongside cash compensation and potentially corporate equity. She does not present a settled strategy for hiring established partners: current hiring is not intended to match their compensation, and that question is deferred.
qs: we only need a small number of people who are believers that they want to be on the journey of something new
some they can get some equity in the ink or we could pay them in cash
eventually to hire partners we'll have to think through that but we're not trying to hire match that salary right now that compensation.

kp.k: Expansion prioritises private markets, with geographic options open
kp.d: Berrent describes a global orientation and plans to deepen investor-side private-market coverage, including direct investments alongside existing fund transactions. London is discussed as an option if US regulation becomes too burdensome. Arizona is suggested by the host and acknowledged by Berrent as possible, not announced as a concrete expansion decision.
qs: we think about going to London a lot
we haven't seen the benefit yet
really sort of going deep in private markets. Every single type of investment we're going to do on investor side, we're going to do directs. We're already doing a variety of fund transactions.

kp.k: Verified legal data shifts control toward clients
kp.d: Berrent reports client appetite for directly querying and analysing lawyer-verified information extracted from long agreements, including comparisons, trends, outliers and negotiating leverage. She frames this as a shift from outside counsel as gatekeepers of legal data and market knowledge toward client control. Her comparison with HR data becoming a business driver is a prediction about legal data's future importance, while client feedback is described as guiding successive features.
qs: taking sort of this idea of the gatekeeper and the owner of legal data and what's market being from outside council to being to a client and that is a very big shift.
now HR data is such a driver of businesses I think legal data will be the same
whatever the answers are, it's been verified by a lawyer.
the format of data that I can graph I can compare I can you know think about I can see trends I can see outliers

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jen Berrent claims that designing narrowly focused legal services around AI enables substantial reductions in time and cost, delivered through transaction-based fixed fees rather than hourly billing.
pts.d: Berrent describes Covenant as an AI-powered law firm serving private-market investors, rather than a conventional firm adding general-purpose efficiency tools. She claims purpose-built, end-to-end processes reduce time and cost by 80–90%. Its basic document review costs $900; she estimates comparable traditional legal work costs roughly ten times more, while acknowledging some firms charge less. Additional lawyer involvement is available for a further fixed fee. The claim concerns selected productized workflows, not all legal services.

pts.k: Berrent claims multiple-model review increases a small legal team's capacity and makes human verification easier.
pts.d: Covenant has six lawyers and sends investment documents to multiple AI models. Berrent describes the low marginal cost of additional model reviews as a substitute for scaling the number of people performing initial review. Agreement between models is said to make verification faster, while disagreement prompts deeper investigation. Her use of 'leverage' refers explicitly to technology and focus, not a reported associate-to-partner staffing ratio. Lawyers remain responsible for verification; this is not a claim of autonomous legal delivery.

pts.k: Berrent claims larger context windows made commercially viable review of complex private-market documents possible.
pts.d: She links Covenant's January 2024 launch to a November 2023 increase in model context-window capacity. In her account, earlier retrieval-augmented generation and chunking approaches lost too much quality on long agreements containing definitions, nuance and cross-references; human review remained faster. This is a claim about the feasibility of Covenant's particular document-review workflow, not a benchmark result for legal AI generally.

pts.k: Berrent claims AI-native providers can take defined document-review work away from traditional firms while leaving bespoke advisory work with specialists.
pts.d: Covenant targets complex work that clients would otherwise send to outside counsel or Big Law, beginning with limited partnership agreement review and expanding to investor-side document review and most-favored-nation election compendia. Berrent argues associates are unnecessary for the initial reading process in this workflow, while remaining valuable for other work. Covenant deliberately does not build a full-service tax or regulatory practice and instead works alongside clients' existing specialist advisers. The claimed substitution is task-specific, not elimination of lawyers or traditional firms.

pts.k: Berrent claims AI-enabled delivery shifts control of legal information from outside counsel to clients and predicts legal data will become a business resource comparable to HR data.
pts.d: She describes clients wanting interfaces through which they can query their own lawyer-verified legal data rather than receive only documents or emails. Structured information extracted from lengthy agreements can be graphed, compared and examined for trends, outliers and negotiating opportunities. She reports current client appetite and predicts a broader shift across industries. Product development, rather than simply adding lawyers, is therefore central to Covenant's expansion.

pts.k: Berrent predicts productized law could capture a SaaS-like share of client spending, but conflicts require separation between opposing-side legal practices.
pts.d: Using Salesforce as an analogy, Berrent suggests clients could consolidate legal use around a productized offering. Covenant limits its law firm to investor-side representation; deploying the technology for the other side would require a different law firm. She describes a New York law firm and sister IP company connected by a technology license, and reports taking external capital for product development. These are her account of the business structure and strategic conditions, not an independently established conclusion about regulatory compliance.

pts.k: Berrent claims personal trust remains important when clients adopt AI-powered legal services, even if subsequent human contact falls sharply.
pts.d: She says Covenant's acquisition process remains relationship-based rather than primarily product-led: she or her co-founder still meets every client to establish confidence in the people and quality behind the service. Technology changes ongoing delivery without eliminating the initial lawyer-client relationship.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of Berrent's founder experience, descriptions of Covenant's operations and reported client feedback.
pts.d: Operational particulars include six lawyers, the $900 basic review price, multiple-model review with lawyer verification, the January 2024 launch and the decision to fund further client-facing product development. The 80–90% efficiency reduction and roughly tenfold price comparison are founder estimates without a disclosed sample, measurement method, comparator dataset or independent assessment. The transcript offers no measured accuracy or verification-time results. Predictions about legal data and client spending draw on client interactions and analogies to HR software and Salesforce, rather than market-wide evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source distinguishes current operations and dated technical milestones from open-ended expansion predictions.
pts.d: The document labels the interview 2026. Berrent explicitly dates the enabling context-window change to November 2023 and launch to January 2024. She describes capital raising and strategic choices as occurring 'this year' or at its beginning, without separately stating a calendar year in those passages. Current savings depend on focused, purpose-built workflows, sufficient context capacity, lawyer verification and avoiding bespoke specialist expansion. Future investor-side coverage and cross-industry data transformation have no quantified deadline. London and Arizona are possibilities discussed, not announced moves; broader data access is described as still in its infancy.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate effects concern private-market investors, their legal teams, traditional outside counsel and Covenant's lawyer workforce.
pts.d: Investor clients receive lower-priced fixed-fee reviews and access to structured, verified information; those without an in-house general counsel can purchase additional lawyer involvement. Covenant's lawyers supervise and verify AI-assisted work rather than expanding initial review through a large associate workforce. Traditional firms face substitution in defined document-review tasks but retain bespoke tax, regulatory and high-value advisory roles. Opposing-side firms are possible technology partners rather than clients represented by the same investor-side practice. The prospective data-control shift extends to corporate clients in other industries. The source does not claim effects on unmet civil legal need or quantify profession-wide employment changes.
